P1-FIXPOINT-SENTENCE: The dispatcher's consolidation hold re-posted a wake-up for every held lane on every call, so the event queue grew with fleet size and, because one dispatch call does not reach a fixed point, the duplicates also changed assignments. The fix, pre-registered as change 5 before any rerun row, posts one wake-up per lane and lot and repeats dispatch at the same instant until nothing changes. Every block of E40, E41 and E42 was rerun with it; the 4,052 earlier rows are archived and reproducible with the fix off, and every number from E40, E41 and E42 in this paper is from the rerun rows. Against the archived row of the same cell, seed and start year, the primary outcome moved by −0.27 h on average and 2.4 h in absolute value in E40 (2,749 rows with a value; at most 153 h in one run, the plan-ahead dispatcher on Earth at 60 % load), by +0.21 h and 6.9 h in E42 (1,170 rows; at most 256 h) and by −0.10 h and 1.6 h in the 132 rows of E41 that existed before the fix (at most 18 h). An earlier version of this section quoted smaller figures; they were for the mean delay per delivery of all cargo and not for the primary outcome. Table C1 in Appendix C gives every tested comparison before and after the fix, as change 5 promised. No verdict changed. The paired differences moved from −0.38 (−1.99 to 1.16) to −0.84 (−2.91 to 0.95) h for H3a, from −2.49 (−4.13 to −1.01) to −2.32 (−3.94 to −0.64) h for H4's linear model, from +91.3 (83.3 to 100.0) to +89.9 (81.8 to 98.7) h for H2 and from +4.2 (3.4 to 5.1) to +5.4 (3.5 to 8.5) percentage points for H6.
P1-RUNS-SENTENCE: Rows are not all distinct runs. Of E40's 2,750 rows, 2,029 are distinct: 721 repeat another row of their cell exactly (the same seed and the same outcomes). 650 of the repeats are the second block of the 13 cells whose regime never waits for Earth (Section 4.6), which no comparison counts. The rest are in cells that do depend on Earth: owners alone on the Moon, whose only use of Earth is the hand coordination of apron conflicts, has 39 distinct runs of 80 at 10 % load, 61 distinct runs of 80 at 30 % load and 71 distinct runs of 80 at 60 % load, and owners alone from Earth, plan ahead at 10 % load has 78 of 80. Table 5 gives the distinct count beside the rows. A further 60 rows of E41 and E42 rerun E40's auction cell by design, as a check that the experiments agree, so the 5,480 rows hold at most 4,699 distinct simulated years.
P1-BOTTOM-MAX-NAME: the relay that is always up and the full-information marketplace
P1-H3A-SENTENCE: the test could not show it. The difference was −0.84 h with a 90 % interval of −2.6 to 0.7 h, which reaches past the margin of ±1.5 h on at least one side, so the auction may be better or worse than the marketplace by more than 10 %, and the data cannot tell.
P1-H3A-VERDICT: The 90 % interval is not inside that margin, so equivalence is not shown and H3a is not supported as stated; the interval includes zero, so the auction is shown neither better nor worse than the marketplace.
P1-H3A-INTRO-CLAUSE: kept urgent cargo waiting 5.6 % less than the full-information marketplace, a difference whose 90 % interval (−17 % to +5 %) includes zero
P1-H3A-ABSTRACT-CLAUSE: came within 0.8 h of the full-information marketplace, not distinguishable from zero but too wide to show equivalence
P1-H1-60-SENTENCE: At 60 % load the same comparison cut the wait by 1,077 h (95 % CI 984 to 1,175 h, n = 30, p < 0.001), so H1's second half, that pooling helps at 60 % load too, is supported (Table 7; the 60 % rows lie outside the Holm family of Section 4.5).
P1-H4-60-SENTENCE: At 60 % load the linear model cut the wait by 31.5 h (95 % CI 25.2 to 38.2 h) and the network's difference, −1.3 h (95 % CI −6.0 to 3.1 h), includes zero (n = 30; Table 7).
P1-GROUPS-60-SENTENCE: At 60 % load the three groups stand in the same order: owners alone 1,144 to 1,630 h, the Earth-losing pooled regimes 80 to 484 h and the on-Moon regimes with the marketplace 45 to 77 h.
P1-H4-LIGHT-CLAUSE: and there the data could show neither a gain nor its absence: the gain's interval (−0.1 to 2.2 h) includes zero and reaches past the ±2 % margin
P1-LEARNED-EVAL-LABEL: evaluation rerun on the corrected engine on 12 November 2026
P1-LEARNED-EVAL-SENTENCE: The evaluation of the learned bids that was first made on 27 October 2026, before the two engine fixes of changes 4 and 5, was rerun on the corrected engine on 12 November 2026 with the same seeds and the same policies; the earlier values are kept in the old file. On its 30 seeds the linear correction changed the urgent wait against hand-built bids by −2.49 h (−4.15 to −0.82 h; −17.7 %) at 30 % load and by −30.3 h (−36.0 to −24.5 h; −40.4 %) at 60 %, in agreement with E40; the network's difference was −0.16 h (−1.61 to 1.30 h) and +5.4 h (−2.9 to 13.6 h), not distinguishable from zero at either load.
P1-GUARD-30-SENTENCE: At 30 % load the same check does not come out clean. On its 10 seeds the urgent wait did not move measurably (−1.23 h, −3.91 to 1.45 h), so on that smaller sample the gain itself is not distinguishable from zero, and the delay of bulk cargo rose (+0.23 h, 0.02 to 0.44 h); the delay of all cargo did not move measurably (+0.18 h, −0.04 to 0.39 h). At the middle load the learned bids therefore make bulk cargo wait a little longer, and we do not claim that their gain for urgent cargo is free for other cargo there.
P1-GUARD-30-CLAUSE: at the middle load a ten-seed check found bulk cargo waiting slightly longer
P1-IMIT-RERUN-SENTENCE: These figures are a record of training: the first imitation round on the tuning seeds, with the engine of 27 October 2026; they were not rerun. On the corrected engine, on the evaluation seeds at 30 % load, the hand-built bids chose the marketplace's item in 88.35 % of rounds, the network's bids in 86.37 % and the linear bids in 70.76 %.
P1-OOD-LABEL-SENTENCE: The cells of Table 6 were rerun on the corrected engine with the rest of that evaluation.
P1-OOD-SENTENCE: Outside its training range the linear model was run in five cells of ten seeds each: two and five owners, message loss 0.25 and 0.40, and light load. It kept the same sign in all five, with an interval clear of zero in three: two owners (−4.95 h, −8.66 to −1.24 h), message loss 0.25 (−2.31 h, −4.29 to −0.34 h) and light load (−1.22 h, −2.12 to −0.31 h). The interval includes zero at five owners (−1.33 h, −3.50 to 0.84 h) and message loss 0.40 (−1.62 h, −4.91 to 1.68 h) (Table 6). A sixth cell, a later start year, is not an out-of-range test and is not counted: the start year changes nothing in these runs, which never wait for Earth, so the cell repeats the guard runs at the middle load value for value. The file of 27 October 2026 mixed engine states: its out-of-range runs were made after a fix that its evaluation and guard runs predate. The rerun file has all three on one engine.
P1-LIN-WEIGHTS-SENTENCE: The largest weights lower the bid, and so favour the item, for the planned hours of the job (+1.93 h per unit, the feature scaled by 1/3), the load as a share of capacity (+1.28 h per unit) and the number of robots heard (+1.04 h per unit), and raise it for the slack to the item's target time (−1.96 h per unit, the feature scaled by 1/10), the hours to drive to the pad (−1.41 h per unit) and the battery's state of charge (−1.39 h per unit); the other weights in each direction are smaller than these.
P1-URGENT-ITEMS-SENTENCE: A run holds few urgent items: on average 15 at 10 % load (from 0 to 31 over all E40 runs), 52 at 30 % load (from 21 to 102 over all E40 runs) and 122 at 60 % load (from 61 to 184 over all E40 runs), counted in the full-information marketplace's block-one runs; one run at light load had none and has no value of the outcome. The light-load results therefore rest on means of about 15 items a run.
P1-SEEDS-ADDED: The rule was not applied: no seeds were added in any cell, and every cell holds the 30 seeds of the design (and the 50 runs of the second block where it applies). Read on each cell's mean of the primary outcome, the 95 % half-width exceeded 10 % of the mean in 29 of the 40 E40 cells: 12 of 12 at 10 % load, 10 of 15 at 30 % load and 7 of 13 at 60 % load (three cells lie within half a percentage point of the threshold, so the count depends that much on the resampling). Read on the paired differences, against 10 % of the reference regime's mean, it was exceeded for H1, H2, H3a and H4 (linear) (for H3a a 90 % half-width of 1.64 h against 1.49 h). By the rule ten more seeds at a time should have been run in those cells. We did not extend any sample after seeing results, so every interval in this paper is from the fixed design of 30 seeds, or of 80 runs where a regime depends on Earth (Section 7).
P1-H3A-RALLY-SENTENCE: The comparison is confounded by the lost-link rule. The on-Moon regimes send an idle robot that nobody hears back to a site the mast sees, 809 times a year in the auction's runs, and the marketplace has no such move. Where the radio reaches every robot the returns fall to 11 a year and the auction's wait is 15.2 h, 0.3 h above the marketplace's and 1.2 h (−0.2 to 2.7 h) above its own default cell (Section 5.5). The auction's small advantage in the point estimate is therefore more likely an effect of that repositioning than of where the decision is made. The marketplace was not run with the same move, so the two cannot be separated here.
P1-E41-LOSS-SENTENCE: With no message loss the four on-Moon regimes kept urgent cargo waiting 14.6 h (the elected leader), 14.3 h (the auction), 13.8 h (the learned network bids) and 10.8 h (the learned linear bids), against 14.9 h for the full-information marketplace on the same seeds; the learned linear bids lay below it by 4.2 h (2.7 to 5.7 h) and the others did not differ from it. Raising the loss to 0.40 added 1.0 h (−0.4 to 2.7 h) for the elected leader, 3.9 h (2.0 to 5.9 h) for the auction, 3.7 h (2.3 to 5.3 h) for the learned network bids and 4.3 h (2.4 to 6.4 h) for the learned linear bids, that is 0.18, 0.67, 0.67 and 1.00 % of the loss-free wait per point of loss. The best allocators in Lott and Honary's benchmark lose about 0.3 % of makespan per point [11]; makespan and cargo wait are different quantities, so the two slopes are set side by side and not compared. The auction and the learned network bids rose above the marketplace at loss 0.40 (one-sided 95 % lower bound of the paired difference above zero); the elected leader and the learned linear bids stayed level with or below it through loss 0.40. Bursty loss at a mean rate of 0.25, against steady loss at the same rate, cut the wait of the auction by 1.4 h (95 % CI 0.4 to 2.4 h) and cut the wait of the learned linear bids by 1.2 h (95 % CI 0.4 to 2.2 h) and left the others within their intervals of zero.
P1-E41-DEPTH-SENTENCE: Bundles of up to five jobs hurt the auction: against depth 1, depth 5 raised the urgent wait by 6.0 h (95 % CI 4.4 to 7.8 h) at loss 0.25 and raised it by 10.0 h (95 % CI 7.7 to 12.6 h) at loss 0.40, and depth 2 raised it by 3.7 h (95 % CI 1.8 to 5.6 h) at loss 0.25 and raised it by 5.0 h (95 % CI 2.3 to 7.6 h) at loss 0.40. Stale claims, bids on items that another robot had already taken by the time the bundle was accepted, rose from 0 to 314 per year at depth 5 and loss 0.40. H3b, that depth 5 is worse than depth 1 at loss 0.25 to 0.40, is supported. For the learned bids at loss 0.40, depth 5 raised the wait of the learned network bids by 9.8 h (95 % CI 7.6 to 12.0 h) and raised the wait of the learned linear bids by 8.7 h (95 % CI 6.4 to 11.1 h). The design has no cell with depth 2 or 5 and no loss, so it cannot say how much of this penalty is due to loss and how much to bundling under this demand; the stale claims are almost the same at loss 0.25 and 0.40 (85 and 86 a year at depth 2, 313 and 314 at depth 5), which points to bundling. The finding of Lott and Honary that the best depth falls under loss [10] can therefore be neither confirmed nor contradicted here.
P1-E41-RANGE-SENTENCE: Radio range mattered less than loss: against the default 5 km range, a 2 km range lowered the auction's urgent wait by 0.1 h (95 % CI −0.2 to 0.0 h), not distinguishable from zero, a 10 km range left it unchanged on every seed and a radio that reaches every robot raised it by 1.2 h (95 % CI −0.2 to 2.7 h), not distinguishable from zero. With the lost-link rule off the wait rose by 3,267.5 h (95 % CI 3,011.7 to 3,540.4 h), and the share of robot-time out of reach of every mast went from 5.1 % to 83.1 % (809 returns to a mast per year with the rule on). A second mast at pad B raised the wait by 1.5 h (95 % CI 0.1 to 3.2 h) and cut that share from 5.1 % to 5.0 %. H3c, that the elected leader matches the auction unless the mesh partitions, was tested in ten cells by equivalence within ±10 % (90 % CI of the ratio): the leader matched the auction under loss 0 and a perfect radio; it differed under loss 0.40 (faster by 2.6 h, 95 % CI 0.7 to 4.5 h) and the lost-link rule off (faster by 871.6 h, 95 % CI 571.3 to 1,149.8 h); under loss 0.10, loss 0.25, bursty loss, a 2 km range, a 10 km range and the second mast the interval was too wide to decide either way.
P1-E41-DEPTH-CLAUSE: Bundle depth 5 made the auction worse at message loss 0.25 and 0.40 (Section 5.5)
P1-CHECKS-SENTENCE: In addition, 121 checks of the engine's phase-5 verification suite (lunarsim/vv5.py, results in results/vv_phase5.json and on the live site's verification page) bear on this paper: 100 verifications that the code does what the model says, 21 validations against references outside the model, by technique: analytic (33), comparison to other models (16), degenerate tests (16), historical data (16), internal validity (15), traces (13), metamorphic testing (7), extreme condition (4), event validity (1). Deterministic identities are held to 10−9 relative or exact; stochastic checks pass when the error is within a tolerance set in advance, and a 99 % batch-means interval that misses the reference is recorded as a bias flag, not a failure; the checks ran at commit a773dea. Their outcomes are in Section 5.11.
P1-FAILED-CHECKS-SENTENCE: Of the 121 phase-5 checks of Section 3.11 tagged to this paper, 6 failed: four are the pairing check D10 (pairing by seed reduces the variance of the difference from the full-information marketplace) for owners alone from Earth with plan ahead, owners alone from Earth, strict, owners alone on the Moon and the strict dispatcher on Earth, whose delay varies mostly between start years (Section 4.5); two are the monotonicity check L5 (the learned bid is monotone in approach time, mass and battery charge) for the network and the linear model. The other 100 that ran passed; 15 were not run, because the check does not apply to this model or was left out, each with its reason in results/vv_phase5.json; one met its tolerance with a 99 % interval that misses the reference, recorded as a bias flag (D4 class 2).
P1-ID-FIX-SENTENCE: After every experiment had run, a verification check found that cargo ids were not unique: 9–18 of about 2,970 items a year reused an earlier id, in every regime (change 10 of the pre-registration). Ids enter the simulator's decisions only through a planning memo within one dispatch call. The fix was tested by rerunning 48 full years (E40, E43: every regime or mode, seeds 1–3), of which 48 gave outcomes identical item by item, compared by content without ids, 39 of them in this paper's experiment; reused ids fell from 670 to 0. No experiment was rerun and no reported number changes; trace and scene files written before the fix still carry the duplicate ids.
P1-CHECK-FINDINGS-SENTENCE: The L5 failures are properties of the trained policies, not of the code: the learned bid was not monotone in approach time, mass and battery for the network in 32 % of the probes and the linear model in 67 % of the probes, as the policies were tuned on urgent wait and not constrained to monotone bids (Section 3.10).
P1-PAIRING-SENTENCE: The pairing holds for demand, landings and initial faults: in the engine's phase-5 checks (D10, Section 3.11) every regime's E40 run had the same demand as the full-information marketplace's on the same seed and start year across 880 regime pairs; the per-job intervention and fault redraws are shared in draw order and diverge once the allocations differ, in every regime. How much the pairing buys was measured at 10 % load, on the mean delay per delivery and not on the primary outcome, over the 80 rows of each cell, which include the repeated runs of the regimes that never wait for Earth. Against the marketplace, pairing cut the variance of the paired difference to 0.00–0.52 of the unpaired sum for B_EARTH plan_ahead, B_EARTH_RELAY 0.8, B_EARTH_RELAY 1.0, C_AUCTION, C_LEADER, C_LEARNED_LIN, C_LEARNED_MLP, and only to 0.90–0.99 for A_EARTH plan_ahead, A_EARTH strict, A_MOON, B_EARTH strict, whose delay varies mostly between start years; their paired intervals are little narrower than unpaired ones would be. A bootstrap over pairs treats the runs of one start year as independent, so for H2 we also give the interval obtained by resampling whole start years (Section 5.3).
P1-E41-REPLICATION-SENTENCE: E41's default auction cell reran E40's auction at 30 % on the same 30 seeds and reproduced every run exactly.
P1-H6-SHARE-SENTENCE: Allowing pairs of different owners raised the share of team items delivered from 12 % to 93 % at team share 0.10 (paired difference 82 percentage points, 95 % CI 78 to 86, n = 30) and from 11 % to 96 % at team share 0.25 (paired difference 86 percentage points, 95 % CI 83 to 88, n = 30) at message loss 0.10. The starting share is an input and not a finding: of the 12.4 team items a year at team share 0.10, 1.5 (12 %) and 28.4 team items a year at team share 0.25, 3.2 (11 %) weigh no more than the one same-owner pair can lift (FLEX with CLV-1, 2,080 kg), by the mass range we assumed, and the same-owner auction delivered 1.5 and 3.0. H6 is registered on “the share of items delivered” and names no team share [43]. The engine's measure is a share of mass, the kilograms delivered over the kilograms ready: it rose by 1.7 percentage points (1.5 to 2.0) at team share 0.10 and 5.4 percentage points (3.5 to 8.5) at team share 0.25. Counted in items, cross-owner pairs delivered 11.8 more items a year (8.0 to 15.7) on 2,920 at team share 0.10 and 80.7 more items a year (28.0 to 168.7) on 2,853 at team share 0.25. Every interval excludes zero, so H6's first part is supported in kilograms and in items. The Holm family tests it on the mass share at team share 0.25, a cell the registration does not name (adjusted p < 0.001, Table 7); 0.10 is the design's default. The gain held at loss 0.25 and 0.40 (Table 8).
P1-H6-MEETINGS-SENTENCE: Failed meetings rose with message loss: at team share 0.25 the auction with the commit step and a 1 h timeout had on average 4.0 failed meetings per year at loss 0.10, 12.1 at 0.25 and 25.2 at 0.40. Without the commit step it had more at loss 0.25 (15.2) and more at 0.40 (35.4): paired by seed, the step cut failed meetings by 3.1 (0.6 to 5.8) at loss 0.25 and 10.2 (4.5 to 16.0) at loss 0.40. That is the direction the second part of H6 names, but it is a property of the model and not an independent measurement. No message is repeated inside a handshake. With the commit step a meeting fails only when the proposal and the answer arrive and the commit is lost; without it a meeting fails whenever the single proposal is lost. If a message gets through with probability s, the two cases have probability s2(1 − s) and 1 − s, and the second is the larger for every s below one. We therefore report the second part of H6 as following from the message count and not as supported by a test. What the runs do measure is the step's price: the urgent wait with it was 1.8 h (0.1 to 3.6 h) longer at loss 0.25 and 9.1 h (6.8 to 11.5 h) longer at loss 0.40, a cost that excludes zero at both losses, because a meeting that the step refuses is a lift that waits. The timeout sets the waiting and cannot buy fewer failures in this model, where a partner that missed the commit never comes: the hours robots spent waiting at meeting points are the failed meetings times the timeout, 6.5 with a 0.5 h timeout, 12.1 with 1 h and 27.7 with 2 h at loss 0.25. The exploratory variant in which the base computer arbitrates each meeting had no failed meetings at either loss. It repeats its message to each vehicle up to 20 times within the timeout, where the commit variant repeats nothing, so that comparison is one of retry budgets and not of protocols.
P1-H6-ABSTRACT-CLAUSE: of the crates that need two rovers, 12 % are within the one same-owner pair's capacity by construction, and pairs of different owners' robots delivered 93 %; a commit step before each meeting cost urgent wait, and its lower count of failed meetings follows from the handshake's message count
P1-H6-SHORT-CLAUSE: Of crates that need two rovers, 12 % fit the one same-owner pair by construction; cross-owner pairs delivered 93 %
P1-LRIP-PATTERN-SENTENCE: Of the 15 messages, nine are published (POSITION, STATUS, INTENT, ALERT, TASK_ANNOUNCE, TASK_STATE, RESERVE_RELEASE, MAP_NOTICE and HELLO), three are requests (TASK_BID, RESERVE_REQ and CAP_QUERY) and three are the responses to them (TASK_AWARD, RESERVE_GRANT and CAP_MANIFEST).
P1-LRIP-V02-SENTENCE: This paper describes version 0.2. Its position report carries east, north and height in the site grid, heading, speed, a one-sigma horizontal value, the navigation source, a moving flag and, in the six bits that version 0.1 left spare, a code for the 95 % horizontal uncertainty on a logarithmic scale; it is still 13 B of content and a packet of 41 B. The frame, the datum and the time scale of a vehicle's positions are not repeated in every report. The vehicle declares them in its heartbeat, HELLO, which grows from 30 B to 32 B and is sent at least every 10 s, and in its manifest, which grows by 9 B. A receiver refuses a position report from a sender that has no authenticated declaration under its current key epoch. Packets of version 0.1 still encode and decode bit for bit. A covariance is not carried: the report states its uncertainty as the one-sigma value and the 95 % code only.
P1-LRIP-MANIFEST-SIZE-SENTENCE: As minified JSON the two example manifests are 1,235 and 1,245 B; in the compact form they are 292 B (small rover) and 289 B (hopper), and the small rover's is a signed packet of 376 B. The design note had estimated 247 and 251 B. The measured sizes are larger mainly because the implementation keeps the owner and model names as text, so that a manifest from an owner the reader has never met still decodes: with the two names replaced by registry numbers the same encoder gives 266 and 268 B.
P1-LRIP-CANDO-SENTENCE: For the small rover above (transport.carry version 1.0, at most 200 kg, interface tray-A), the rule accepts a carrying task of 150 kg and refuses one of 250 kg, one that asks for version 1.1 or 2.0, and one that needs an interface the manifest does not list. The hopper's manifest lists transport.hop and no transport.carry: it is refused for every carrying task and accepted for a hop with 5 kg. A vehicle with no manifest is refused.
P1-LRIP-VECTORS-SENTENCE: The release holds 45 golden packets: every message in the narrow-band profile with authentication (12 with the 8 B code, 3 signed), the same 15 without security, and 15 in the broadband profile, each as hexadecimal bytes with the field values it must decode to, and the two example manifests in compact form. The keys in the file are test keys. The broadband vectors carry the 8 B code; the 16 B code that Table A1 gives for broadband has no vector yet.
P1-LRIP-CAPFILTER-SENTENCE: With manifests generated from the vehicle classes, switching the filter on changed none of the 128 summary values of a 45-day run of the auction (one run, seed 3, message loss 0.10), because those manifests state exactly the capacity the engine already checks; with no manifests at all, deliveries fell below 10 % of that run's. This is not the check that the companion papers quote, in which every option added for the protocol is switched off and the run equals the earlier engine's in 144 summary values over 30 days on seed 2 [44, 45].
P1-E53-H13-SENTENCE: With authentication on and 20 rovers, the busiest link carried 8.37 kbit/s at one position report a second (95th percentile over the 30 draws; mean 7.96 kbit/s), inside the 16 kbit/s of the earlier budget, and 67.4 kbit/s at ten a second, above it. H13 is on the predicted side of the threshold in both clauses, and we report it as a design calculation and not as a test [54]. Its first clause is arithmetic on the sizes and rates we assumed and holds in any geometry: reports are not relayed, so no node can hear more than the fleet's sum, 20 × 0.418 kbit/s = 8.37 kbit/s, which is the 95th percentile above. The design note from which the second pre-registration took its parameters had already computed 49 B/s per robot, 7.9 kbit/s for 20 robots and 65.6 kbit/s for their position reports alone at ten a second, for the first version of the protocol; E53 gave 7.86 kbit/s with that version's sizes, and the heartbeat that carries the declaration in version 0.2 raises it to the 8.37 kbit/s above.
P1-LRIP-INTRO-SENTENCE: By the sizes and rates we assumed, twenty rovers reporting once a second offer 8.37 kbit/s, inside the 16 kbit/s we had budgeted, and 67.4 kbit/s at ten reports a second, which does not fit. This is a design calculation and not a test, and it holds only on a channel that the base schedules, with reports travelling one hop (Section 5.8).
P1-LRIP-CONCLUSION-SENTENCE: the periodic reports and the task and road messages of 20 rovers offer 8.4 kbit/s at one authenticated position report a second, which fits a 16 kbit/s channel only if the base schedules it and reports travel one hop
P1-E53-AUTH-SENTENCE: Without authentication the same link carries 5.46 kbit/s and 44.3 kbit/s: the security header and code add 53 % to the load at 1 Hz and change neither side of the comparison.
P1-E53-FRAMING-SENTENCE: These are packet sizes before link framing and channel coding. Inside a Proximity-1 frame every message gains 12 B (a synchronisation marker, the frame header and a checksum, as our design note counts them from the Proximity-1 standards [58]): a rover then offers 67.9 B/s and 20 rovers 10.9 kbit/s, a scheduled channel must run at 13.6 kbit/s, and the 16 kbit/s channel is full at 23 rovers and not at 30. Channel coding is counted in neither figure.
P1-E53-TYPES-SENTENCE: The traffic model holds 11 of the 15 message types: TASK_ANNOUNCE, CAP_QUERY, CAP_MANIFEST and MAP_NOTICE are not in it, so the count is of the periodic reports and the task and road messages and not of the full message set.
P1-E53-DRIVING-SENTENCE: Two further calculations, with the same sizes, show how far the result depends on its inputs. Only 2.6 % of the vehicle-steps in the pool that the fleet geometry samples are driving steps. Drawn from those alone, 20 rovers are 1.58 hops from the base on average where a path exists, 93 % of them have one, and the busiest link carries 6.3 kbit/s at one position report a second (95th percentile), against 1.01 hops, 99 % and 8.4 kbit/s for parked vehicles. As scheduled airtime the driving draws need 7.85 kbit/s, or 10.19 kbit/s in Proximity-1 frames, and on slotted random access 17.1 kbit/s or 22.2 kbit/s, which does not fit. Over the recorded month of Section 5.9 a vehicle had a path to the base for 57 % of its driving time. If the status and intent reports are also sent once a second, the 20 rovers offer 20.03 kbit/s at the sources, 25.98 kbit/s framed, which is above the 16 kbit/s channel in every case, before any airtime is counted: H13's first clause holds only at the report rates we assumed.
P1-LINKLAW-SENTENCE: Nor does the link law enter this paper's runs: a link exists or it does not. As a calculation outside them, the companion paper's link budget [44] gives two rover antennas 5 km apart 1,574 kbit/s over flat ground and 701 kbit/s when the Moon's curvature is counted (5.0 dB more loss), so the 5 km range we assume is a range at which a narrow-band channel closes and a megabit channel may not.
P1-E53-AIRTIME-SENTENCE: Load at the sources is not airtime (Proposition 2). On a channel that the base schedules, with a fifth of the time left as guard intervals (efficiency 0.8, Assumed), the 8.37 kbit/s of 20 rovers needs a channel of 10.46 kbit/s, which fits 16 kbit/s. On slotted random access, whose efficiency tends to 1/e, it needs 22.7 kbit/s, which does not fit; and if every report were relayed once, the scheduled channel would need 20.9 kbit/s, which does not fit.
P1-PROP2-EXAMPLE-SENTENCE: With E53's sizes and rates a rover offers 52.3 B/s, so N = 20 gives L = 8.37 kbit/s. With h = 1: R ≥ 10.46 kbit/s on a scheduled channel (η = 0.8) and 22.7 kbit/s at η = 1/e; with h = 2 on the scheduled channel, 20.9 kbit/s.
P1-E53-NMAX-SENTENCE: This geometry draws positions from the trajectories of the eight simulated vehicles with every vehicle-step equally likely, so the draws follow where the fleet spends its time, which is near the base, and that sampling is why the busiest link hears the whole fleet (mean hops to the base 1.01 to 1.03; 97 % to 99 % of rovers with a path to it), so the scheduled 16 kbit/s channel is full at 30 rovers reporting once a second. Vehicles on the road are placed differently, as the next paragraph shows.
P1-E53-10HZ-SENTENCE: At ten reports a second even five rovers load it with 16.9 kbit/s. The 1,000 kbit/s broadband channel carries 80 rovers at ten reports a second (268 kbit/s as load, 335 kbit/s as scheduled airtime).
P1-E53-SPREAD-SENTENCE: With the same number of rovers spread uniformly over the route samples, radio neighbourhoods are smaller. The busiest link carried about half the fleet's summed load, 41 % to 49 % on average over draws and 52 % to 80 % at the 95th percentile: 4.83 kbit/s for 20 rovers at 1 Hz against 8.37 kbit/s near the base. A scheduled 16 kbit/s channel then carries 40 spread rovers at 1 Hz and not 80. The price is reach. Events took 1.1 to 2.2 hops to the base where a path existed, and only 30 %, 43 %, 62 %, 83 % and 93 % of 5, 10, 20, 40 and 80 rovers had one. A sparse fleet spread over the routes is cut off from the base before its radio channel fills (Table 10).
P1-E54-DESIGN-SENTENCE: The month is July 2028 as the engine recorded it for the auction at the middle load, with the fleet of eight vehicles and the road rules of [45], on 30 seeds (199 jobs and 88 single-lane road reservations a seed). Three ways of carrying the messages are compared at per-hop loss 0.10, 0.25 and 0.40. Drop and retry sends end to end along the current shortest path, again every 180 s, at most 5 times and never past the message's lifetime. Store and forward moves a message hop by hop with custody [60]: a lost transmission is repeated after 10 s while the link lasts, a message with no path waits in a 64 MB store, and it expires at its lifetime. Both sets of retry settings are Assumed and were not swept: the baseline's five tries end 12 minutes into a lifetime of 60 minutes, while store and forward repeats for all of it. The third adds the lost-link return of Section 3.13: a vehicle that has had no path to the base for 600 s retraces its path at half speed to the last point where it had one. The messages are generated from the recorded run: an award to each vehicle of a job (its lifetime is the lease of 1 h, the time after which an awarded job returns to the pool; an award that expires undelivered is a lost job, auctioned again), a reservation grant with every award (lifetime 60 s; 6,028 grants against the 2,628 single-lane reservations of the recorded runs, so more than half of them belong to jobs with no such reservation), a report at the end of each job, and a status report every 10 s for the base's age of information. A 14-day Earth blackout is imposed on days 8 to 22, as H14 names it. It can affect only messages addressed to Earth, which here are the daily records of who did what (the ledger); awards, grants, reports and status travel between the base and the vehicles and do not depend on it.
P1-LRIP-LADDER-SENTENCE: The example manifest of Section 3.12 carries these times for its vehicle: 30 s without the base before it treats itself as cut off, 600 s held before it returns, 3,600 s at the last link point before it leaves for the meeting point.
P1-E54-H14-SENTENCE: At per-hop loss 0.25, drop and retry lost 10 of 6,028 awards, 0.33 jobs a seed (95 % CI 0.17 to 0.53). Store and forward lost 2, and none when unheard vehicles were assumed to return to their last link point. The paired difference between the third and the first is −0.33 jobs a seed (95 % CI −0.53 to −0.17, n = 30), which excludes zero: the first clause of H14 holds against this baseline. The baseline decides much of that. Drop and retry gives up after five tries, 12 minutes into a lease of 60 minutes, while store and forward can repeat 360 times in the same hour; neither setting was swept. Paths are almost always one hop (a mean of 1.01 to 1.03 hops to the base in E53), so custody at relays plays little part, and five independent losses in a row have probability p5: 6,028 × 0.255 = 5.9 of the 10 lost awards, 62 of the 85 lost at loss 0.40 and 0.06 of the 4 at 0.10. The others are vehicles that had no path for the whole lease, of which store and forward itself lost 2. The comparison is therefore mostly one of five tries in 12 minutes against 360 tries in an hour, and a baseline that retried every 10 s without a cap was not run. The 14-day Earth blackout that H14 names cannot affect this clause (Section 4.8).
P1-E54-H14-VERDICT: first clause holds against the stated baseline; second clause not testable as written
P1-E54-STUCK-SENTENCE: H14's second clause, that the rule leaves no reservation stuck past its timeout, is not testable as written, and we report no verdict on it [54]. The zero that the results file holds for it follows from the rule as first written, under which the base released a silent vehicle's reservation at its timeout. That rule is withdrawn: releasing the segment is unsafe if the vehicle is disabled inside it. Under the rule of Section 3.13 the segment is marked unconfirmed and may be entered only at caution speed. What the replay gives is a count. Without the return to the last link point, 2,566 of the 2,628 reservations in the 30 seeds ended while their holder had no path to the base 60 s after the timeout. In the replay every vehicle had left its segment on schedule, but the base cannot know that, so these segments stay unconfirmed until the holder is heard again: 7,349 h in all, 245 h a seed. How many stay unconfirmed when vehicles return to their last link point was not counted, and what crossing an unconfirmed segment at caution speed costs in delay is not priced.
P1-E54-GRANTS-SENTENCE: One further difference is a consequence of two settings and not a finding. A reservation grant lives 60 s and drop and retry repeats after 180 s, so it has one try on one hop and loses grants at the per-hop loss rate itself: 9.5 %, 25.6 % and 39.9 % at loss 0.10, 0.25 and 0.40. With custody, 2 of 6,028 grants were lost at loss 0.25 (0.03 %), and none with the return to the last link point. These are counts of messages: a grant was generated for every award, and more than half of the jobs have no single-lane reservation (Section 4.8), so a lost grant here is not a vehicle stopped before a segment.
P1-E54-COST-SENTENCE: The return is applied by editing the contact plan while the recorded job timeline stays: for the radio a returning vehicle stands at its last link point, and for the logistics it is driving its job at the same time. The replay therefore counts what the return gains in contact and not what it costs in interrupted jobs. That cost is not small: the rule produced 82 returns a seed against 199 jobs, and in the recorded month a vehicle had a path to the base for only 57 % of its driving time, so the ladder of Section 3.13 read literally would interrupt a large share of drives.
P1-E54-V02-SENTENCE: The replay E54 was repeated at the packet sizes of version 0.2 and in Proximity-1 frames, and no value and no verdict changed. That is a property of the replay's message set and not a test of version 0.2: it sends task awards, reservation grants and task states, whose sizes version 0.2 does not change, and a size counts only against a node's store of 64 MB.
P1-E54-AOI-SENTENCE: The return to the last link point changes what the base knows, not what the radio loses. Without it the base's picture of a vehicle was on average 88 min old (5,287 s) under either transport, and the worst-placed vehicle went unheard for 31 h. With it the mean age was 45 s and the worst vehicle's 149 s: the return was made 82 times a seed and removed 336 vehicle-hours of isolation a seed. The end-of-job reports show the cost of holding a message: drop and retry lost 32 % of them, store and forward lost 1.4 % and delivered the rest 543 s late on average, because a vehicle that ends a job out of reach waits for a contact, and with the return to the last link point the delay fell to 33 s.
P1-E54-LEDGER-SENTENCE: The daily ledger bundle to Earth was replayed over 61 days (31 bundles; the replay does not depend on the seed, and the file repeats it for each), in which the longest stretch without Earth was 24.8 days (the imposed blackout together with the natural gaps next to it). Drop and retry lost 94 % of the bundles whatever their lifetime. Store and forward lost 35 % with the 14-day lifetime first chosen and none with a lifetime of 25.8 or 30 days: the lifetime of an Earth-bound bundle must exceed the longest stretch without Earth, a sizing rule for the network's design [44].
P1-E54-LEDGER-DESIGN: The Earth-bound ledger, one bundle of 10 kB a day (Assumed), is replayed separately over 61 days with lifetimes of 14, 25.8 and 30 days.
P1-P6-FAMILY-SENTENCE: Both sit in that file's confirmatory family with H9′, H10′ and H15a, which are reported in the companion paper [45]. The registration asks for Holm's procedure [52] across all five. It is applied at α = 0.05 to the three that have a sampling test, H10′, H14 and H15a; H9′ and H13 are comparisons with a threshold and are listed without a test, which is a change from the registered family. For the correction H14 is tested by an exact sign test on the lost jobs per seed. That test was added after the results were seen; the registered rule, a paired interval that excludes zero, gives the same verdict [54].
P1-E54-HOLM-SENTENCE: In the family of the second pre-registration, the difference in lost jobs is tested by an exact sign test over the 30 seeds: fewer with store and forward and the return in 9 seeds, more in none, the same in 21 (one-sided p = 0.002; two-sided p = 0.004). Holm's correction over the three hypotheses of that family with a sampling test gives an adjusted p of 0.004 on the one-sided p and 0.008 on the two-sided one, so the first clause of H14 stands after the correction, against the baseline described above. Of the other two, H15a is supported (adjusted p at most 0.003) and H10′ is not supported as a whole (adjusted p = 0.93); both are reported in the companion paper [45].
P1-E53-DRAWS-SENTENCE: That each clause held in every one of the 30 draws carries no information for the first clause, which no draw could have failed. H13 has no sampling test, and Holm's correction of the second pre-registration's family does not include it.
P1-E54-ABSTRACT-CLAUSE: drop-and-retry capped at five tries lost 10 of 6,028 awards at 25 % message loss; store-and-forward that retries for the whole lease lost 2, and none when unheard vehicles were assumed to return to their last link point
P1-E54-SHORT-CLAUSE: drop-and-retry capped at five tries lost 10 of 6,028 awards at 25 % loss, store-and-forward 2, and none when unheard vehicles were assumed to return to their last link point
P1-E54-AOI-CLAUSE: the base's picture of a vehicle was 88 min old on average without the return to the last link point and 45 s with it, a gain counted without the jobs the return would interrupt
P1-PROP3-EXAMPLE-SENTENCE: At per-hop loss 0.40 over three hops the mean age of a 1 Hz report is 4.2 s and it exceeds 29 s one time in a thousand; for a direct neighbour at loss 0.25 the two figures are 0.84 s and 5.0 s.
P1-PROP3-E54-SENTENCE: E54's ages are of kind (b): the worst vehicle's 31 h without the lost-link rule is its longest stretch with no path to the base, and the rule shortens that stretch to 149 s (Section 5.9).
P1-PROP4-EXAMPLE-SENTENCE: The protocol's heartbeat is 1 s: a vehicle sends HELLO whenever it would otherwise send nothing in a second (Table A2). With k = 5 (Assumed), a failed vehicle is marked silent after 4.5 s on average and at most 5 s. One rover watching one live rover raises 0.78 false marks a day at loss 0.10 and 531 at 0.40; keeping them below one a day needs k = 5, 8 and 12 at loss 0.10, 0.25 and 0.40. Being marked silent does not hand the job over. By Section 3.13 the base marks the vehicle failed only after a second, longer timeout or a sighting, and the design gives that timeout no value; a silent vehicle's job returns to the pool when its lease ends, at most 60 min after it was last heard with the lease of E54. With that lease, two auction rounds of 10 s, a new winner 1.5 km away at 4 km/h, and cargo aboard the failed rover with probability 0.5 and a 1 h transfer (all Assumed), the expected extra wait is up to 60 min + 20 s + 22.5 min + 30 min = 112.8 min, about 1.9 h. If a sighting confirmed the failure at once it would be 4.5 s + 20 s + 22.5 min + 30 min = 52.9 min. Detection and auction are seconds in both cases, so a shorter heartbeat would buy nothing; the lease sets the wait.
P1-PROP4-EARTH-SENTENCE: With gaps of 11 days and windows of 16 days at this base [42], the wait for Earth alone is 53.8 h, 29 times the hand-over on the Moon with the lease and 61 times the one after a sighting.
P1-PROP6-DEFINITIONAL-SENTENCE: What the count proves is limited. For seven of the nine fields (e, n, h, speed, sigma_h, moving and u95_code) the number of values is two to the power of the field's bits, because we set the range by the bit width; for those the lower bound is definitional. Only heading and nav_src have a count that is not a power of two, which is why the joint count is 103.4 bits, which rounds up to the 104 the layout uses. The steps are also not matched to one another: the position step is 1 cm and the step of its own uncertainty 5 cm. A coarser position step or a smaller site grid would save bits, so 13 B is the size of this layout and not a lower bound for a position report in general.
P1-LRIP-ABSTRACT-SENTENCE: The robots' 15 message types are written down and their encoding implemented: an authenticated position report is a 41 B packet before link framing and coding; by calculation 20 rovers reporting once a second offer 8.4 kbit/s, which fits a 16 kbit/s channel only if the base schedules it and reports travel one hop
